strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: distilling large image datasets without expensive unrolled optimization. Combining class-specific feature prototypes with per-class BatchNorm regularization provides a plausible, practical synthesis pipeline.

Table 1 reports strong results at moderate and larger image budgets. On ImageNet-1K, WMDD achieves 57.6% and 60.7% accuracy at 50 and 100 images per class, compared with CDA's reported 53.5% and 58.0%.

The evaluation includes three benchmarks, multiple compression budgets, three-run accuracy estimates, component ablations, and regularization sensitivity. Table 2 demonstrates useful transfer to larger ResNets, reaching 62.2% on ImageNet-1K with ResNet-101 at 50 images per class.

The overall pipeline is understandable, with pseudocode and synthesis hyperparameters. The manuscript credits its principal datasets, optimal-transport tools, and SRe2L/DeepInversion foundations, and acknowledges teacher dependence and inherited dataset biases.
weaknesses: The central formulation does not establish the claimed conceptual novelty. With the implemented squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized support weights, Eq. (7) reduces to standard k-means quantization: minimizing the average squared distance from each real feature to its nearest prototype. There is only one target distribution per class. The paper neither explains this equivalence nor compares against k-means prototype inversion with identical regularization, leaving the benefit of its barycenter machinery unclear.

The headline improvements are difficult to attribute to Wasserstein matching. Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L on ImageNet at 10 images per class, whereas Table 3's stated baseline obtains 36.1%; this discrepancy is not reconciled. Moreover, holding cross-entropy and per-class BatchNorm fixed in Table 3, adding the barycenter term changes accuracy by only -0.1, +0.8, and +0.5 percentage points on ImageNette, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet, respectively. Matched training protocols and corresponding ablations at 50/100 images per class are needed to substantiate the central contribution.

The MMD comparison does not isolate the proposed explanation. Section 5.5 removes augmentations and FKD but does not establish identical feature extractors and regularization across methods. At one image per class, the squared-Wasserstein optimal prototype is simply the class feature mean, also targeted by linear-MMD mean matching in the same feature space. Thus, the reported 5.77% versus 0.48% cannot establish the claimed geometric advantage without further controls. General criticisms of MMD also overlook characteristic kernels that distinguish full distributions.

The optimized probability masses are disconnected from the final distillation procedure. Algorithm 2 learns weights, but Eq. (16) and Algorithm 1 retain only prototype locations; their use in student sampling or training is unspecified. Uniformly training on the resulting images generally represents a different measure from the weighted distribution optimized in Eq. (7), weakening the distribution-matching justification.

The solver description has technical and reproducibility gaps. The quadratic/Hessian argument in Section 4.2.2 applies with a fixed transport plan; the minimized transport objective is generally nonconvex in support locations. Algorithm 2 updates the weights and then reuses a plan computed with the previous marginals, without justification. It also permits zero weights while the position update divides by those weights. Initialization, step-size policy, and stopping criteria for barycenter optimization require specification. These issues need correction or clarification to make the implemented optimization reproducible.

The efficiency evidence is too narrow for the ImageNet-scale claims. Table 6 evaluates only ImageNette at one image per class, where the optimal prototype reduces to a mean. It does not establish transport overhead at larger support sizes or provide an end-to-end breakdown covering teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, synthesis, and relabeling.
